AbstractText.Label: CONTEXT
AbstractText.content: Palliative care for the older person is often limited, resulting in poor quality of dying. Pharmacological management can be one of the components to achieve better symptom control.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVES
AbstractText.content: To describe the anticipatory prescription of medication for symptomatic treatment and the deprescription of potentially inappropriate medication during the last days of life.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: This was a cross-sectional descriptive study between October 1, 2012 and September 30, 2013 in 23 acute geriatric wards in Flanders, Belgium. Structured after-death questionnaires were filled out by the treating geriatrician for patients hospitalized for more than 48 hours before dying.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Anticipatory prescription of medication was present in 65.4% of cases, 45.5% of the cases was prescribed morphine, 15.5% benzodiazepines, and 13.8% scopolamine hydrobromide. A deprescription of potentially inappropriate medication was noted in 67.9% of cases. The likelihood of anticipatory prescription was significantly higher in cases where death was expected (odds ratio [OR] 19; 95% CI 9-40; P < 0.0001) and significantly lower where dementia was present (OR 0.35; 95% CI 0.16-0.74; P < 0.006). The likelihood of deprescription was higher in cases where death was expected (OR 20; 95% CI 10-43; P < 0.0001) and in cases of patients dying from an oncological disease compared with those dying from frailty or dementia (OR 7.0; 95% CI 1.1-45.6, P = 0.042).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Anticipatory prescription of medication and deprescription of medication at the end of life in acute geriatric wards could be further optimized. A well-developed intervention to guide health care staff in patient-centered pharmacological management in the last days of life seems to be needed.
